title: Network Service Discovery
summary: Network service discovery is the mapping step in which an adversary enumerates listening services on remote hosts and network devices to find something worth attacking or moving toward. The work is done with port scans, service and version probes, and wordlist scans that reach every address in a range and record which ports answer, which are filtered, and what banner or response each one returns. Because the probes are read-only and never complete a real session, the activity produces no authentication events on the target; it shows up instead as a large volume of half-open connections from one source, sequential or sweeping destination addresses, and repeated connection attempts to ports the environment never uses. Discovery is not limited to the local subnet: cloud instances are scanned from other cloud hosts, and where cloud and on-premises networks are connected, an intruder can reach services outside the cloud. On macOS networks the same goal can be met through Bonjour service advertisements. Detection is strongest when network flow data, firewall denies, and host connection logs are correlated, and when the scan is linked to what follows, such as exploitation attempts or authentication failures.

beginner.definition: Network service discovery means finding out which services are running on other computers in a network. The attacker sends small test messages to many addresses and records which ones reply. The replies show which doors are open and what is behind them.
beginner.whyItMatters: You cannot attack a service you do not know exists. Scanning finds the old, forgotten or unpatched systems that people forgot about. The scan itself usually raises no login alerts, because no login happens. What the scan learns makes every later step easier, so earlier detection is valuable.
howItWorks: The attacker chooses a range of addresses, and sometimes every port on every address.
Small probe messages are sent to each port, and the replies are timed and recorded.
Open, closed and filtered results are compared, which shows which services are listening.
Service and version probes ask each open port to identify itself and its software version.
The results are saved as a map of hosts, ports and services for later targeting.
On some networks the attacker can simply listen to service announcements instead of probing.
beginner.example: Think of a courier checking every front door on a long street. They knock at each one, note which doors are unlocked, and write down the nameplate beside each. They never enter any house and never show a fake identity. Later, the list tells them exactly which homes to visit at night.
takeaways: A port scan is reconnaissance: it is loud on the network but silent in the logs of the target.
Correlate firewall denials, flow records and host connection attempts to spot sweeping probes.
Reduce the value of scanning by closing unused services and keeping an inventory of what should be exposed.

objectives: Define network service discovery and describe the kinds of probes it uses.
Explain why a port scan generates little or no authentication telemetry on the target host.
Identify the network and firewall data sources that reveal scanning activity.
Explain how cloud networks and service announcement protocols change the discovery picture.
Apply service inventory and minimisation as defences that limit the value of scanning.
